I won't recommend a bike, but I will offer some general advice.

1) Slow speed control is highly underrated. It's entirely different from control at higher speeds, and it's fun, and it's easy to practice. Start here: https://motorcycletraining.com/team-arizona-riding-tip-february-2013-slow-speed-turning-technique/

2) Get a good full face helmet with good ventilation. Make sure it fits right. Stash a twenty under the liner in case you run out of gas somewhere and left your wallet at home.

3) One of those warm things that fits over your neck is worth as much as a second jacket in the cold. In a pinch, putting newspapers between your jacket and your body will keep you warm, too. Remember, there is no such thing as bad weather, there is only being underdressed.

4) Riding in the rain is dangerous and uncomfortable. If you're going to tour, get great at it before you go.

5) It's only a matter of time before you go into a turn too goddamn fast. When it happens, lean further. Most of the time, you'll be amazed at how tight you can turn when you really have to. The rest of the time you'll lo-side, which is safer than hi-siding anyway. Never quit, and never look at the thing you don't want to hit. Put your eyes on daylight and fly it all the way to the end.

6) Once you stop hitting turns too fast, and figure out that gravel, broken pavement, farm vehicles, children on bikes and turtles (yes, fucking turtles) are waiting just beyond your sight on every curve, then turns will stop being your number one hazard. At that point, it's cars. They will hit you when you are sitting still at an intersection. They will turn into you. They will lane change into you. They will lie in wait in parking lots for you. Your only weapons are agility and unobstructed vision, and they only work if you are very good at being agile, and paying attention. Did I mention low speed handling? Become great at that stuff.

6) Never tailgate. Daylight is life.

7) Check your tire pressure all the time. A soft tire is very bad news on a bike, and slow leaks happen.

8) Be ready to fall in love with the damn thing. Go where it takes you.

As far as beginner bikes, you could get a sport-type bike like the Yamaha R3, Honda CBR300, or Kawasaki's new Ninja 400. Having smaller engines, they are good on gas and cheap on insurance. And they're super fun to ride. They have a more upright riding position as well, so you're not just leaning on the handlebars all the time.

I personally prefer sport bikes, and being newer, they have fuel injection - which is awesome. And some of them have ABS.

For cruisers, you're looking at something with a bigger engine because sport bikes make their power in the high revs but cruisers need torque. You will save some money here as well, because you'll be looking at something used. A Honda VLX600 or Yamaha Virago 535 would be great beginner cruisers. Not heavy and cumbersome, enough power to be a ton of fun, and you can pick them up for very little. They are carburated though, if that doesn't bother you.

I'd recommend not getting something super powerful (especially sport bikes) or super heavy (cruisers). When you're beginning, something light but with enough get-up-and-go to put a smile on your face! Look in your local classifieds for used bikes. You can pick many of these up for a great price.

Look into bikes with an upright sitting position if you were thinking cruiser. Sport touring bikes or naked streetbikes like the FZ07 are lighter and easier to handle than big cruisers. They still can go pretty fast, but they're not going to do it by accident like a CBR1000 might for a new rider

Lingonberries are quite bitter and a bit dry, not sweet at all. Did not know you could make pies with them, around here they are usually made into an unsweetened jam and served as a side-dish with meatballs, meatloaf etc. Not a fan myself, but apparently quite popular.
So basically the Scandinavian version of cranberries, I guess.

Hehe I was going to compare them to cranberries, but then I realized I'm not sure I have ever tasted cranberries except for sweetened cranberry juice. Lingonberries grow wild everywhere here in Scandinavia so I guess that's why they're more popular.

Cranberries are weird. When you dry them, they have the same texture as a raisin and are more tart and berry-flavoured. When they're fresh they have a fairly dry, odd spongy texture, owing to the inner structure, which is full of little air pockets. They're very tart. I've never liked cranberry sauce, and I only like them in baking if there's a decent amount of sugar involved. Cranberry juice...I only drink it if it's mixed with grape juice.

I did see a jar of lingonberry sauce in my local grocery store last Christmas. I should try some this year. Maybe it's good!
